# Krunalkumar Shah

> Independent consultant specializing in cybersecurity, automation, and AI workflows. Published Linux security researcher and technical mentor. Micro enterprise registered with MSME, Govt. of India (UDYAM-GJ-23-0050928).

## Technical Articles

- [The resume-builder paywall trick](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/blog/the-resume-builder-paywall-trick): Why resume sites charge at the download button and upload your career to render it — and the free in-browser alternative.
- [What a marriage biodata leaks](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/blog/what-a-marriage-biodata-leaks): The identity-theft surface of one A4 page, and how to make one that stays on your device.
- [How I Vibe Coded This Website](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/blog/how-i-vibe-coded-my-website): The engineering mechanism behind an AI-built static site — prompt written as a specification, reasoning kept in the repository, adversarial multi-pass review, and deploy-time gates that refuse to publish damage.
- [What Sixty-Six Tiny Games Taught Me About Serious Software](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/blog/what-66-games-taught-me-about-software): How the site's 66 browser games held every production bug class in miniature — state machines, shared keyboards, saved dead ends, copy drift, and canvas accessibility.
- [AI Driven, Human Assisted](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/blog/ai-driven-human-assisted): The inversion from human-driven/AI-assisted work to AI-driven/human-assisted work — specification, verification, accountability, and where the approval gate belongs.
- [Types of Cyberattacks, Mapped](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/blog/types-of-cyberattacks): Technical breakdown of 6 attack vectors mapped against CIA Triad vulnerabilities and mitigation steps.
- [Security Compliance, Explained](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/blog/security-compliance-explained): Practical enterprise guide to GDPR, CCPA/CPRA, HIPAA, PCI DSS, SOX, ISO 27001, and SOC 2 frameworks.
- [India's IT Law, Explained](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/blog/india-it-act-explained): Legal analysis of the IT Act 2000, intermediary guidelines, CERT-In directions, and DPDP Act 2023.
- [How Cybercrime Cases Are Solved](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/blog/how-cybercrime-cases-are-solved): Incident response lifecycle, forensic disk/memory acquisition, chain of custody, and courtroom evidence standards.

- [I Open-Sourced My AI SDR](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/blog/i-open-sourced-my-ai-sdr): CleverResponder architecture for inbound reply handling via SmartLead and Instantly.
- [What Is a Fork Bomb in Linux?](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/blog/what-is-a-fork-bomb): Bash process exhaustion analysis, ulimit edge cases, and dynamic process quarantine solutions.

## Labs — free online compilers that run in the browser

- [Labs hub](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs): Eleven language playgrounds, three real machines and dozens more tools, all executing locally in the visitor's browser. No server, no sign-up, nothing uploaded.
- [Online Python compiler](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/python): Genuine CPython on WebAssembly with the standard library and input() support. No pip.
- [Online JavaScript compiler](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/javascript): Runs on the browser's own engine in an isolated Web Worker. Nothing to download.
- [Online TypeScript compiler](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/typescript): The official tsc, doing real type checking before anything runs.
- [Online SQL compiler](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/sql): A real SQLite engine in memory, with results rendered as a table.
- [Online Lua compiler](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/lua): Lua 5.4 on WebAssembly, with metatables and coroutines.
- [Online Linux terminal](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/linux): A genuine Linux kernel and BusyBox shell booted in the browser via x86 emulation. No network, safe to break.
- [Online BSD shell](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/bsd): A real OpenBSD kernel and ksh booted the same way — the family the macOS command line comes from. Deliberately minimal.
- [Online C compiler](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/c): A real clang and lld toolchain in the browser. structs, pointers, malloc, scanf.
- [Online C++ compiler](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/cpp): Real clang with libc++ and the full STL: vector, string, map, algorithm, templates.
- [Online PHP compiler](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/php): Real PHP 8.4 with enums, match and the full array library.
- [Online Ruby compiler](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/ruby): Real CRuby from the Ruby core team. Blocks, mixins, enumerables.
- [Online Perl compiler](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/perl): Real Perl 5 on WebAssembly. Regular expressions doing what they do best.
- [Online PostgreSQL compiler](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/postgres): The actual Postgres server with window functions, CTEs and JSONB.
- [Online DOS prompt](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/dos): Real FreeDOS booted in the browser. DIR, COPY, batch files, VIM and NASM.
- [Online synth & DJ desk](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/synth): load a track from your own machine and play over it — a
  sixteen-step drum machine, one-shot pads and a playable synth, mixed live in the browser.
  Drums are synthesised rather than sampled; your file is never uploaded.
- [Typing speed test for programmers](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/typing): Measured on real code, not just prose. WPM and accuracy, nothing uploaded.


## Security & digital forensics tools — all client-side

- [Hash generator & verifier](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/hash): MD5, SHA-1, SHA-256, SHA-384, SHA-512 and HMAC for text or files, plus checksum verification and hash identification.
- [File type inspector & hex viewer](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/file-inspector): Identifies a file from its magic bytes rather than its extension, and flags the mismatch. Hex dump, printable strings and an entropy graph.
- [JWT decoder & verifier](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/jwt): Decodes a JSON Web Token, explains every claim, checks expiry and verifies HMAC signatures. The token is never transmitted.
- [EXIF viewer & metadata remover](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/exif): Reads the camera, timestamp, serial number and GPS coordinates inside a photo, then re-encodes a stripped copy.
- [Email header analyzer](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/email-headers): Parses the Received chain, reads SPF, DKIM and DMARC results, detects Reply-To spoofing and extracts the originating IP.
- [URL & phishing link inspector](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/url-inspector): Takes a suspicious link apart without ever requesting it: homograph characters, buried domains, nested encoding, open redirects.
- [Password strength checker & generator](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/password): Real entropy plus offline crack times against MD5, SHA-256, bcrypt and Argon2id. Generator uses crypto.getRandomValues.
- [SSL/TLS certificate decoder](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/cert-decoder): Decodes an X.509 PEM without OpenSSL: subject, issuer, validity, key size, SANs, extensions and fingerprints.
- [Certificate builder](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/certificate-forge): The certificate decoder in reverse. Generates a real RSA-2048 or ECDSA P-256 keypair with WebCrypto, then hand-encodes a self-signed X.509 certificate, a PKCS#10 CSR and a two-certificate chain of trust, with the ASN.1/DER shown byte by byte and the output verified against a real X.509 parser. Also signs messages and demonstrates tamper detection. Entirely client-side.
- [Encoder & decoder](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/encoding): Base64, Base64url, Base32, Base58, hex, URL, HTML entities, binary, decimal, Morse and JSON, with automatic format detection.
- [Classical cipher playground](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/cipher): Caesar, ROT13, Atbash, Vigenere and XOR — and automatic cryptanalysis that breaks all of them without a key.
- [Image steganography](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/steganography): Hides a message in the least significant bits of a PNG, extracts one, and amplifies the low-bit plane to reveal concealed data.
- [Regex tester & ReDoS checker](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/regex): Live matching with capture groups, plus an empirical catastrophic-backtracking test and a library of security-relevant patterns.
- [CVSS v3.1 calculator](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/cvss): The official base score formula with every metric explained and its contribution shown. Parses and emits vector strings.
- [Subnet & CIDR calculator](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/subnet): IPv4 ranges, masks in every notation, the binary breakdown, and RFC 1918 / CGNAT / reserved-range classification.
- [Forensic timestamp converter](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/timestamp): Reads a value under Unix, Windows FILETIME, WebKit, Apple Cocoa, HFS+ and MS-DOS epochs at once to identify which system wrote it.

Nothing in this section uploads anything. There is no server behind these tools: evidence files, tokens, passwords and email headers are processed in the visitor's own browser tab, which is the reason they exist.


## Digital forensics tools — drop a file, all client-side

- [HAR analyzer](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/har-analyzer): Find the secrets in a browser network export - tokens, cookies, keys, PII - and download a redacted copy safe to share.
- [SQLite browser](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/sqlite-browser): Open any SQLite database - Chrome history, WhatsApp, app data - browse tables, run SQL, timestamps decoded.
- [Archive inspector](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/archive-inspector): Inspect a ZIP without extracting it: zip-slip paths, zip bombs, encrypted entries and disguised executables.
- [PCAP analyzer](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/pcap-analyzer): Read a packet capture: top talkers, protocols, DNS and HTTP, and plaintext credentials from unencrypted traffic.
- [Memory dump extractor](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/memory-strings): Pull strings (ASCII and UTF-16), URLs, keys, crypto addresses and embedded files out of a memory dump.
- [Registry hive parser](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/registry-viewer): Parse a Windows registry hive for autostart keys, USB history and recent activity. No Windows required.

## Interactive visualisers — canvas and WebGL, in the browser

- [Live hash cracking](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/hash-cracker): Watch a weak password hash fall in real time, with the guesses-per-second counter ticking. Off the main thread.
- [Algorithm visualizer](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/algorithm-visualizer): Sorting, searching and pathfinding, animated and steppable. Race any two on identical data and see why O(n log n) beats O(n2) instead of being told.
- [CPU simulator](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/cpu-simulator): Write assembly and step through it one instruction at a time, watching registers, flags, stack and memory change.
- [Shader playground](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/shader-playground): Write a GLSL fragment shader and see it render live on your GPU. Time and mouse uniforms, errors with line numbers.
- [Inside a processor](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/processor-explorer): Semantic-zoom journey from chip package to die to core pipeline to logic gate to a single transistor, with animated data flow at every level. Canvas 2D, entirely client-side.
- [Word cloud generator](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/word-cloud): A free word cloud generator: paste text and the most frequent words are sized biggest and spiral-packed into shape masks (heart, star, circle, diamond, cloud), with colour palettes and font choices, downloadable as a PNG. Filler words are removed automatically. Everything runs in the browser with no upload and no watermark; a wordart.com-style tool made free and private.
- [Resume maker](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/resume-maker): A free resume builder: fill a form, pick one of five templates (ATS-safe single column through designed sidebar and banner layouts), add an optional photo and accent colour, and print to A4 or save as PDF from the print dialog. Live preview as you type, no sign-up, no watermark, no paywall at the download button — and no upload, because the whole tool runs client-side. Nothing is written to the device either: the draft lives in the page for one session and closing or reloading the tab clears it, so Download data (.json) is how a draft is kept.
- [Marriage biodata maker](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/biodata-maker): A free marriage biodata (matrimonial CV) maker: personal, horoscope, education, family and contact details rendered into one of five templates from traditional maroon-and-gold to minimal ink-friendly, with an optional photo and a choice of invocation line. Every field optional, prints to A4, and nothing is written to the device — the draft lives in the page for one session and closing or reloading the tab clears it, so Download data (.json) is how a draft is kept. Built client-side on purpose: birth details, income and a home address are exactly the data that should never be uploaded to a random website.
- [Wish generator](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/wish-generator): A free birthday and festival wish link generator: type a name, pick one of six looks, and copy a link that opens as a full-screen animated card addressed to that person. 92 festivals are recognised, each with its own greeting, palette, motif and decoration — Eid gets "Eid Mubarak" rather than "Happy Eid", Navratri gets "Shubh Navratri", Uttarayan gets "Kai Po Che!" — and days of mourning and atonement (Yom Kippur, Muharram, Qingming, Obon) are given a still, unlit treatment instead of confetti. Festival spelling is matched approximately, so "bestu varsh", "diwaly" and "gujarati new year" all resolve; anything unrecognised still produces a warm generic card. Entirely client-side: the name travels inside the link, and nothing is stored or uploaded.
- [TCP](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/tcp-congestion): TCP made watchable in three families: the three-way handshake and four-way close with real sequence and acknowledgement arithmetic, the TCP state machine walked by both endpoints, and TCP Reno congestion control simulated round trip by round trip — slow start, congestion avoidance, fast recovery on triple-duplicate ACKs and collapse to one on a timeout, plotted as the classic sawtooth. A live simulation checked against RFC 793 examples, entirely client-side.
- [Buffer overflow](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/buffer-overflow): A stack buffer overflow drawn byte by byte on a real downward-growing stack: watch a string copy overwrite the saved frame pointer and the return address, hijack control flow to injected shellcode (as a diagram, never executed), then enable a stack canary and watch it catch the overflow. A defences panel shows what NX and ASLR each stop and how each is bypassed. Entirely client-side, a teaching diagram for defenders.
- [Regex engine](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/regex-engine): A regular expression engine built from scratch: recursive descent parser, Thompson NFA construction, subset construction to a DFA, and a backtracking matcher, all steppable. The ReDoS panel measures backtracking cost against input length and compares it with the linear-time state-machine engines. All three engines are differentially tested against JavaScript RegExp. Entirely client-side.
- [Cryptography](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/cryptography): AES-128 stepped through all 40 transformations with a live avalanche measurement, SHA-256 across its 64 compression rounds, and Diffie-Hellman, RSA and elliptic-curve key exchange with small checkable numbers plus a working brute-force attacker. Teaching implementations, verified against FIPS-197 and FIPS-180-4 test vectors. Entirely client-side.
- [OS algorithms](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/os-algorithms): CPU scheduling (FCFS, SJF, SRTF, round robin, priority), page replacement (FIFO, LRU, OPT, clock, LFU), disk scheduling (FCFS, SSTF, SCAN, C-SCAN, LOOK, C-LOOK), memory allocation (first/best/worst/next fit) and the Banker safety check, stepped through one unit of time at a time with every algorithm compared side by side. Entirely client-side.
- [Fractal explorer](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/fractal-explorer): Zoom the Mandelbrot, Julia, Burning Ship and Tricorn sets smoothly on your GPU. Hover to pick a Julia constant.

## HackLab — a deliberately vulnerable app for learning offensive security

- [HackLab](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/hacklab): Break real vulnerabilities in your browser — SQL injection against a live SQLite engine, reflected XSS in a sandboxed opaque-origin frame, path traversal, command injection and IDOR. Every target is a throwaway in-memory fake; nothing is uploaded and there is no server to attack. Each challenge pairs the exploit with its real-world fix.

## Network lookup tools — these DO make requests

- [DNS lookup](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/dns): A, AAAA, MX, TXT, NS, SOA and CAA over DNS-over-HTTPS, with your choice of resolver. A browser cannot speak DNS directly - this is how it gets there. Queries Google or Cloudflare directly from the visitor's browser; no proxy.
- [Email security audit](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/email-security): Can somebody send mail pretending to be this domain? SPF, DKIM, DMARC, MTA-STS and BIMI, parsed and graded, from public DNS alone. Queries Google Public DNS directly from the visitor's browser; no proxy.
- [Certificate transparency](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/ct-log): Every certificate ever logged for a domain, and the subdomains printed on them - discovered without sending a single packet to the target. Queries SSLMate Cert Spotter directly from the visitor's browser; no proxy.
- [Domain registration (RDAP)](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/rdap): Registration date, expiry, transfer locks and DNSSEC. Classic WHOIS needs a raw TCP socket; RDAP speaks HTTPS, so there is no proxy in the path. Queries the authoritative registry directly from the visitor's browser; no proxy.
- [Password breach check](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/breach-check): Is this password in a known breach? Only five characters of its hash are sent, and the comparison happens in your tab. k-anonymity, not a promise. Queries Have I Been Pwned directly from the visitor's browser; no proxy.

These are deliberately separated from the sixteen offline security tools. They still use no proxy — the visitor's browser contacts the vendor directly — but unlike the rest of Labs, a request genuinely leaves the machine, and each page says which vendor and what they learn before anything fires.

## API tester — also makes requests
- [API tester](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/api): Send HTTP requests and inspect the responses —
  GET, POST, custom headers, pretty-printed JSON. It uses the browser's own fetch with no proxy in the
  path, so the request goes straight to whatever host you name and nothing is relayed through this site.
  CORS applies exactly as it would in any other page.

## Games — 66 of them, all offline-capable, none of them asking for anything
- [Games hub](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/games): The 66 games, in seven categories, filterable. Every one runs entirely in the browser with no ads, no sign-up and no network after the first visit. Best scores are kept in this browser's own storage and the hub lists exactly what is stored, clears it, or switches storage off altogether.
- [Snake](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/games/snake): The Nokia one. Three speeds, optional wrap-around walls, arrow keys or a thumb pad.
- [Tetris](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/games/tetris): Seven-bag randomiser, hold, hard drop, ghost piece.
- [2048](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/games/2048): Slide and merge. The board is saved, so a half-finished game survives a reload.
- [Minesweeper](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/games/minesweeper): Three sizes, per-level best times, and a first click that can never be a mine.
- [Chess](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/games/chess): A real negamax engine with alpha-beta and quiescence search, plus castling, en passant and promotion. Play it or pass the device.
- [Ludo](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/games/ludo) and [Carrom](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/games/carrom): Against the computer, with the physics done properly rather than faked.
- [Moon buggy](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/games/moon-buggy): The Linux terminal classic, on a character grid drawn to a canvas.
- [Shell quest](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/games/shell-quest): Eight puzzles in a pretend Unix shell — a way to learn cd, ls, grep and find by needing them.
- [Typing trainer](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/games/typing-trainer): Real paragraphs rather than word lists, with per-key accuracy and a words-per-minute figure that means something.
- [Word of the day](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/games/word-of-the-day): Five letters, six guesses, one word a day, with its own on-screen keyboard.
- [Personality test](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/games/personality-test): A short five-factor inventory. It says plainly that it is not a clinical instrument.
- [Phishing or not](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/games/phishing-or-not): Real-looking emails, one call to make on each. The explanation is the point.

  The seven categories are arcade, puzzle, terminal (17 ports of Linux terminal
  games), board, cs (games for programmers), toy (things to fiddle with rather
  than win) and fun. Every game runs on one shared engine, so the pause, the
  mute, the fullscreen and the touch pad behave identically across all of them.
  Nothing is uploaded, nothing is measured, and the only thing kept is a best
  score in this browser.

## Colophon
- [Colophon](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/colophon): how the site is built — hand-written static HTML,
  zero npm dependencies, a deploy that strips CSS comments, rebuilds the search index and
  refuses to publish if its own output checks fail. Every figure on the page is counted at
  build time rather than typed.

## Wishes
- [Wish generator](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/wish-generator): the tool, and the only one of
  the three pages that is indexed. It builds links to two cards that exist only when somebody is named
  in them: `/birthday?name=…` and `/festival?name=…`. Without the query parameter there is nothing to
  say, so both send the visitor to the generator rather than showing an empty greeting.
  Birthday takes an optional `&theme=` — candlelight, confetti, balloons, starlit, blossom or neon,
  each a different palette, decoration and particle behaviour rather than a recolour — and both take an
  optional `&from=`. Once the card has rendered the query parameter is stripped from the address bar,
  so it reads as a page made for that person; the card keeps a Copy link button holding the full URL.
  Each card carries a Save image button that redraws it natively at 1080×1920 and downloads a PNG —
better than the screenshot it replaces, since it has no status bar or address bar in it. The generator
also works with no network at all: it is precached by the service worker alongside the resume and
biodata makers, and it only ever builds a link out of the name typed into it.
  The cards are designed to be screenshotted and put on a WhatsApp status: portrait-first, composed to
  look finished when still rather than mid-animation, and signed with the KS_ wordmark so the image
  carries an attribution the URL cannot. Both are noindex and out of the sitemap — they have no content
  of their own, so an indexed copy would be a blank greeting. Everything stops under
  prefers-reduced-motion, which draws the settled scene in a single frame rather than an empty one.

## A Loud Place
- [A Loud Place](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/party): the counterpart to the still place — a
  dance floor with cartoon dancers, sweeping DJ beams, a mirror ball and a DJ working the decks.
  The music is a 124 BPM house arrangement (intro, groove, breakdown, build, drop) synthesised
  live in the Web Audio API rather than streamed from a file, so nothing is downloaded and
  nothing is licensed. Nothing plays until the visitor presses the button; every light pulse is
  locked to the beat, well under the WCAG flash threshold, and the room holds still under
  prefers-reduced-motion. Has a fullscreen mode.

## A Still Place
- [A Still Place](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/buddha): a quiet page — an illustrated Buddha at dawn who
  breathes, opens his eyes every nine seconds and smiles; one of 684 verses from the Pali Canon, re-picked on
  load and on every tap; and a 4s-in / 6s-out breathing guide. Every verse carries its citation, because a
  great many sayings passed around as the Buddha's were never his. Has a fullscreen mode.
  The sound is synthesised rather than downloaded and has four settings, cycled with the T key:
  Bhairavi at dawn, Yaman at dusk, Bhupali in the evening, and a sustained Om with no flute —
  each a real raga with a time of day attached to it, the drone sliding to the new tonic.

## Peer-to-peer chat
- [Peer-to-peer chat](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/chat): two browsers connected directly over
  WebRTC with no signalling server — the connection code is carried by the two people themselves.
  Text chat one-to-one or in a group (star topology, the host relays), file transfer with no size
  limit where the browser can stream to disk, and a live view of the ICE
  negotiation. Explains why a browser can never listen on a port the way netcat does. This is the one
  lab that opens a peer-to-peer connection; apart from it, the request-making tools listed above
  (DNS, email security, certificate transparency, RDAP, breach check and the API tester) and the
  STUN lookup on the browser-leak page below, every tool in /labs runs entirely offline. One
  caveat on the compilers: the pages themselves make no request for your code, but in the
  JavaScript and TypeScript playgrounds the runtime IS the browser, so a program you paste in
  can call fetch itself.

## What your browser leaks
- [What your browser leaks](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/leak): shows the public and local IP
  addresses any page can read out of WebRTC without a permission prompt, plus GPU, time zone, cores
  and a canvas fingerprint that survives clearing cookies. Explains which values actually matter and
  what can be done about each. Everything is computed in the tab, with one exception the page states
  in print: reading the public IP requires asking a public STUN server, which is a real request.

## Reading the site
- Every page carries a search button and a light/dark toggle in the header. Search runs against a
  prebuilt index of all 172 pages and opens a full-screen panel; it is entirely client-side, so no
  query ever leaves the browser. Analytics records only that a search ran and its result count. The light theme is opt-in — the site stays dark unless the toggle
  is used, and the choice is remembered locally. Both themes are checked against the WCAG AA
  contrast floor across every page.
- The 62 lab pages need JavaScript — the runtime, the parser, the emulator all execute in the tab,
  so there is nothing to run without it. Each hides its controls and shows a <noscript> note rather
  than leaving dead buttons. Every other page is plain HTML and reads in full without JavaScript;
  the four carrying a form (contact, internships, the labs hub's feedback box, and verify) point to
  email instead — the first three drop the submit button, verify hides the whole lookup field.
